title: Almanac
description: Short seasonal notes on the sky, the garden and the weather. A Day News demo feed.

items.content_html: The September equinox falls on September 22 or 23. On that day the Sun stands directly above the equator, and day and night are close to equal in length almost everywhere on Earth. It marks the start of astronomical autumn in the Northern Hemisphere and spring in the Southern.
A full moon rises at about sunset and sets at about sunrise. It sits on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun, which is why its whole face is lit and why it stays up all night.

Chrysanthemums bloom in autumn because they measure the night. Once nights grow longer than a critical length, the plants switch from growing leaves to forming flower buds, a response to day length called photoperiodism.

Autumn leaves do not gain their yellow and orange; they reveal it. Pigments called carotenoids are in the leaves all summer, hidden by green chlorophyll. As the days shorten and trees stop making chlorophyll, the green fades and the other colors show through. The reds come from anthocyanins, which many trees make fresh each autumn.

On a dark, moonless autumn night, look for a faint smudge of light in the constellation Andromeda. It is the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, and one of the most distant things you can see without a telescope.
Barn swallows gather on wires and rooftops in late summer before they migrate. Swallows that nest in Britain spend the winter in southern Africa, a journey of around 10,000 kilometers each way.
